description: We are a multidisciplinary team of passionate and driven individuals with a shared interest in technology, science, and space exploration. Combining our skills in problem-solving, creativity, research and innovation, we aim to develop impactful solutions to real-world challenges using NASA's open data and resources. We believe in collaboration, curiosity, and pushing the boundaries of what's possible turning bold ideas into practical solutions for a better understanding of our planet and beyond.
summary:
Ribbon is a web tool that answers a lunar mission planner's question, "the landing date moved: is the site still good?", with one picture. It unrolls the full circle of horizon around a landing site into a strip, draws the real skyline from NASA laser-altimeter terrain, and draws where the Sun and Earth travel against it. Near the south pole the Sun circles the horizon about 12° a day, so the width of a mountain on the strip is the number of days it hides the Sun: the picture reads as a calendar.

Ribbon compares two landing plans and says, for each, whether sunlight, the view of Earth, the battery and contact through NASA's Deep Space Network hold for the whole stay, what fails and why, how long the landing can slip, and the next date that works. Around it: a power and contact timeline, an area map, a 3D view and an all-sites calendar, at both poles, in the browser.

NASA picks south-pole landing sites only after launch dates are set, and a slip of a few days can cost sunlight or contact with Earth. Ribbon shows every date at once, and we checked it against NASA's own data.
details:
"We slipped three days. Do we still have sunlight and a radio link to Earth for the whole mission, and if not, when is the next date that works?"

At the lunar south pole that question is hard. The Sun and Earth stay within a few degrees of the horizon, so a hill several kilometres away can decide whether a solar-powered lander gets power and whether it can talk to Earth. NASA says landing sites and dates cannot be chosen separately. When it announced the Artemis III candidate regions in 2022 it wrote: "Specific landing sites are tightly coupled to the timing of the launch window, so multiple regions ensure flexibility to launch throughout the year." In 2024 it added: "The agency will select sites within regions for Artemis III after it identifies the mission's target launch dates, which dictate transfer trajectories, or orbital paths, and surface environment conditions." The cost of getting it wrong is real: when NASA cancelled the VIPER rover in 2024, SpaceNews reported Joel Kearns of NASA's Science Mission Directorate explaining that a launch slipping beyond November 2025 "would require waiting 9 to 12 months until the right lighting conditions return at the landing site in the polar region."

What Ribbon shows

One strip per landing plan. Left to right is the compass: south, west, north in the middle, east, south again, as a panorama photo from the lander would look. Up is elevation above level.

- The skyline, computed from NASA terrain every 0.1° of azimuth out to 200 km over the curved Moon. Ridges in front of the skyline are drawn inside the ground, brighter when nearer, so the strip has depth. A pale strip along the skyline shows how much it changes if the site lies anywhere within its position uncertainty.
- The Sun band, in amber: every place the Sun can be over the coming months. Wherever the skyline rises into the band, there will be dates when the Sun is hidden.
- The Sun's path for this landing, with a tick for each day after landing: solid where the whole disc is up, faint where terrain hides part of it, dotted where it is hidden.
- Earth's region, in blue: Earth hardly moves in the lunar sky; it wobbles inside a small box. If the skyline cuts the box, there are times with no direct link.
- Dark spans, labelled in hours or days.

Below each strip, a timeline of panel output, battery charge and contact with each Deep Space Network complex (Goldstone, Canberra, Madrid) hour by hour, and a strip of every landing time over the next year coloured by what fails.

Around the comparison: the site in 3D at true scale, lit and shadowed by the computed Sun, seen from above or from the lander; a 10 km map of 10,000 points around the site with the share of time in sunlight or with Earth in view, where a click makes a point plan B or draws a rover route that is checked hour by hour; a calendar of all 23 real-terrain south-pole sites against every day of the year; 13 IAU-named craters at the north pole and the highest point near each; a one-page report or the hourly numbers as CSV; and a six-step tour. Every setting lives in the link, so a comparison can be shared.

Why a picture, not a table

Of twelve competing projects we read, at least nine draw a skyline panorama with Sun and Earth tracks; that is the established way to show this data. None of them uses the strip itself as the time axis. Ribbon's idea is that near the pole the horizon is the calendar: the Sun's band shows every date at once, so you see not only whether one date works but which dates will, and why.

What a comparison gives you

Two strips stacked, each with a verdict that names the cause, the direction and the distance of the terrain responsible, and one sentence comparing them. Plan B can be the same site some days later, the same date at another site, or anything else. Observer height (1, 2, 5 or 10 m, from a rover camera to a mast) and three mission profiles set the rules:

- Short stay (6.5 days): continuous sunlight and Earth in view, from NASA's Artemis III planning ("All 13 regions contain sites that provide continuous access to sunlight throughout a 6.5-day period – the planned duration of the Artemis III surface mission"), plus contact every hour and a 20% battery reserve.
- One lunar day (14 days): like today's solar-powered CLPS landers.
- Long rover mission (100 days): VIPER's plan.

The power model is deliberately generic: a 2 m² panel at 25% efficiency turned to the Sun, a 2,000 Wh battery and a 150 W load, with sunlight scaled by the Sun's distance from the solar constant in NASA's Earth Fact Sheet. Every rule and size can be changed in the app, and the app says which numbers are NASA's and which are ours.

The story the app opens on

The highest point of Malapert Massif, one of the nine Artemis III candidate regions NASA listed in 2024, with a 6.5-day stay and the observer 2 m up. We found it by searching every real-terrain site and landing time for a plan A that works and a plan B that fails at all 16 points around the site, so the result does not hang on the exact coordinates.

- Plan A, landing 2027-03-15 18:00 UTC, works: the Sun stays up the whole stay, Earth is in view throughout, the battery stays full and there is contact every hour. The landing can slip up to 24 hours and still work.
- Plan B, the same site three days later, fails. Earth sinks a little lower each day; 4.7 days after landing, ground 0.5 km to the north hides it for the last 44 hours of the stay, so there is no contact with the Deep Space Network. The next landing that works is 19 June 2027, 92.5 days after plan B.

The Sun is up for the whole stay in both plans: here it is Earth, not sunlight, that decides.

Your own point, and real landings

Either plan can be any point, typed as latitude and longitude or clicked on a map. Inside 80°S the skyline is computed in the browser from a 480 m version of the NASA LOLA grid and labelled indicative: hills smaller than about half a kilometre disappear. Outside the terrain the Moon is treated as a smooth sphere, and the app says so.

Three real landings can be replayed: IM-1 Odysseus, IM-2 Athena and Blue Ghost Mission 1. Each loads the real site and landing time, and a short caption keeps what the app shows apart from what happened, with the limit that matters (IM-2 ended on its side in a small crater whose walls a 20 m grid may miss).

How it is built

- Terrain: south, NASA Goddard's 2023 south-pole elevation model (20 m per pixel, from 80°S to the pole) and NASA LOLA 240 m beyond; north, NASA LOLA 10 m, 20 m and 240 m. Skylines are ray-marched every 0.1° of azimuth out to 200 km over the curved Moon, at four observer heights and at 16 points around each site, precomputed for 49 sites (13 MB). The 3D view and the area maps load terrain tiles only where needed.
- Sun and Earth: computed in the browser with the open-source astronomy-engine library plus our own conversion to each site's horizon, including parallax for Earth. The visible fraction of each disc is measured against the skyline, not just its centre.
- Deep Space Network: the three 70 m antennas at the positions in NASA's DSN Telecommunications Link Design Handbook (810-005); contact needs Earth in view from the lander and the Moon at least 6° up at a complex.
- Eclipses: Earth's disc with a 75 km opaque layer of atmosphere, as NASA's eclipse predictions use.
- App: a static web page (Vite, React, TypeScript, three.js for 3D). Heavy work runs in background workers. No server, no account, no tracking.
- Tests: 168 automated tests, including comparisons against JPL Horizons tables, NASA's eclipse table, and two real missions.

What we checked, and what we found

- Sun and Earth directions against JPL Horizons, six site-and-period cases, 6,610 rows per body: the largest difference is 0.0078° for the Sun and 0.0034° for Earth.
- The Moon seen from the three Deep Space Network complexes against JPL Horizons: largest elevation difference 0.0008°.
- Eclipses: all 10 lunar eclipses in NASA's 2027-2030 table (F. Espenak) found, each within 1 minute of NASA's time, with none extra. A plan whose stay includes one gets a sentence in its verdict.
- Date-by-date sunlight and Earth view at Malapert Massif against ACT's Artemis III Geotechnical maps in LROC QuickMap (2 m pixels, every 6 hours through December 2025, built from NASA Goddard's 5 m site elevation models and LROC camera elevation models): at ground level our Sun verdict agrees in 97.7% of 25,425 point-and-time cases, and Earth in 98.7%.
- Long-term sunlight against NASA Goddard's average-visibility maps, ground level: south pole, 23 sites, correlation 0.93 for the Sun and 0.96 for Earth, median difference 1.4 and 0.2 percentage points; north pole, 24 points, correlation 0.975 and 0.998, median difference 0.34 and 0.24 points.
- The Shackleton-de Gerlache connecting ridge against Barker et al. (2021): on average 64.8% of the Sun's disc in view at 1 m and 89.6% at 5 m, against their published 67-71% and 83-89%.
- Real missions. Blue Ghost Mission 1: Ribbon puts sunset 347.8 hours after landing; Firefly reported 346 hours of operations in daylight. IM-1 Odysseus: the Sun's centre reaches a smooth horizon on 2024-03-03 at 08:11 UTC, consistent with Horizons (+0.6° at 00:00 that day, −1.5° a day later).

Where we disagree with NASA's maps: at ground level our long-term sunlight runs about 6 points darker than NASA Goddard's south-pole maps on average, most at ridge crests (the largest gap is 36.5 points, at Shackleton rim's highest point). The 20 m terrain sees relief right next to the point that the maps' 60 to 240 m pixels smooth over, and the low Sun is hidden by it. Against the finer 2 m maps at Malapert, agreement rose from 95.2% on our earlier terrain to 97.7% on the 2023 model.

What Ribbon does not do

- It cannot see relief smaller than its terrain grid (20 m near the south pole).
- Typed points use a 480 m grid, so their skylines are indicative only; sites outside the terrain coverage use a smooth sphere and are labelled.
- Contact is a line of sight to the Deep Space Network, not a link budget: antenna scheduling, relay satellites, terrain at the stations and signals bounced off terrain are not modelled.
- The power model is generic, not a particular lander's.
- Lighting in the 3D view is computed, not a photograph.

Who it is for

Mission planners checking a date slip; CLPS payload teams who need to know their power and communication windows; reviewers and students who want to see why polar landing sites are so date-sensitive; and anyone curious why a lander at the Moon's south pole can lose the Sun or Earth for days behind a hill.

What comes next

LRO camera imagery as an option in the 3D view and the map. A link budget for real antennas. Finer terrain from NASA Goddard's site models where they exist.
